passed.title: Expr.str.contains treats the pattern as a regex unless literal=True
passed.trap: `Expr.str.contains` compiles `pattern` as a regex by default, like pandas `str.contains(regex=True)`. Metacharacters in a plain search term change its meaning. For example, `"1.2"` also matches `"112"` and `"1+2"` because `.` matches any character. A pattern that is not a valid regex, such as `"1+("`, raises an error with the default `strict=True` and turns every row into null with `strict=False`. When you mean a plain substring, pass `literal=True`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"ver": ["1.2", "112", "1+2"]})
out = df.select(
    regex=pl.col("ver").str.contains("1.2"),
    literal=pl.col("ver").str.contains("1.2", literal=True),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

try:
    df.select(pl.col("ver").str.contains("1+("))
    print("no error")
except Exception:
    print("invalid regex raised an error")

lenient = df.select(pl.col("ver").str.contains("1+(", strict=False))
print(lenient.to_series().to_list())
plain = df.select(pl.col("ver").str.contains("1+(", literal=True))
print(plain.to_series().to_list())

passed.title: Expr.str.replace changes only the first match, unlike pandas
passed.trap: pandas `str.replace` replaces every occurrence. `Expr.str.replace` defaults to `n=1` and replaces only the first match, so the other occurrences are silently left in place. Use `Expr.str.replace_all` to replace every match. Both methods treat `pattern` as a regex unless `literal=True`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"d": ["2024-01-15", "1999-12-31"]})
out = df.select(
    first_only=pl.col("d").str.replace("-", "/"),
    every=pl.col("d").str.replace_all("-", "/"),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: Use Expr.str.join instead of the deprecated Expr.str.concat, and note its empty default delimiter
passed.trap: `Expr.str.concat` is deprecated; use `Expr.str.join` instead. The default `delimiter` changed from a hyphen to an empty string, so a straight rename glues the values together. Both methods collapse the whole column into a single value. With the default `ignore_nulls=True`, they also silently drop nulls. Pass `ignore_nulls=False` if a null anywhere should make the result null.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"tag": ["a", None, "c"]})
print(df.select(pl.col("tag").str.join()).to_series().to_list())
print(df.select(pl.col("tag").str.join("-")).to_series().to_list())
out = df.select(pl.col("tag").str.join("-", ignore_nulls=False))
print(out.to_series().to_list())

passed.title: Expr.str.len_bytes counts bytes, not characters
passed.trap: pandas `str.len` counts characters; in Polars that is `Expr.str.len_chars`. `Expr.str.len_bytes` is faster, but it returns the UTF-8 byte length. That length differs as soon as the text contains non-ASCII characters, so length filters built on it silently keep the wrong rows. Use `Expr.str.len_bytes` only when the data is known to be ASCII.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["Zo\u00eb", "Bob", "\u6771\u4eac"]})
out = df.select(
    n_bytes=pl.col("name").str.len_bytes(),
    n_chars=pl.col("name").str.len_chars(),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))
by_bytes = df.filter(pl.col("name").str.len_bytes() == 3)
by_chars = df.filter(pl.col("name").str.len_chars() == 3)
print(ascii(by_bytes.to_series().to_list()))
print(ascii(by_chars.to_series().to_list()))

passed.title: Expr.str.find returns a byte offset, or null when not found
passed.trap: `Expr.str.find` returns the byte offset of the first match, and null when there is no match. It does not return a character index or -1 as pandas does. `Expr.str.slice` counts characters, so feeding it the result of `Expr.str.find` gives off-by-N substrings on non-ASCII text. `Expr.str.find` also treats the pattern as a regex unless `literal=True`. To cut at a delimiter, use `Expr.str.extract` or a split instead of combining find and slice.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["caf\u00e9: 5", "cafe: 5", "none"]})
pos = pl.col("s").str.find(":", literal=True)
out = df.select(
    pos=pos,
    wrong_key=pl.col("s").str.slice(0, pos),
    right_key=pl.col("s").str.extract(r"^([^:]*):", 1),
)
print(ascii(out.to_dict(as_series=False)))

passed.title: Expr.str.strip_chars strips a set of characters, not a prefix or suffix
passed.trap: `Expr.str.strip_chars` and `Expr.str.strip_chars_end` treat `characters` as an unordered set of characters. Every leading or trailing character in that set is removed, so stripping `".csv"` can eat into the file name itself. To remove an exact string, use `Expr.str.strip_suffix` or `Expr.str.strip_prefix`. Also, once you pass `characters`, whitespace is no longer stripped unless you include it in the set.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"f": ["report.csv", "docs.csv", "vcs.csv", "data.csv "]})
out = df.select(
    as_set=pl.col("f").str.strip_chars_end(".csv"),
    as_suffix=pl.col("f").str.strip_suffix(".csv"),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: Expr.str.split_exact and Expr.str.splitn return structs and use n differently
passed.trap: Both methods return a `Struct`, not a list; use `Expr.str.split` if you want a list. In `Expr.str.split_exact`, `n` is the number of splits, giving n+1 fields, and anything after the n-th split is not kept in any field. In `Expr.str.splitn`, `n` is the maximum number of items, and the last field holds the remainder. pandas `str.split(n=1)` therefore corresponds to `Expr.str.splitn(by, 2)`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["a_b_c", "d"]})
exact = df.select(pl.col("s").str.split_exact("_", 1)).unnest("s")
print(exact.to_dict(as_series=False))
n1 = df.select(pl.col("s").str.splitn("_", 1)).unnest("s")
print(n1.to_dict(as_series=False))
n2 = df.select(pl.col("s").str.splitn("_", 2)).unnest("s")
print(n2.to_dict(as_series=False))
print(df.select(pl.col("s").str.split("_")).to_series().to_list())

note.title: A dollar sign in the replacement value is a capture-group reference
note.trap: In regex mode, `$name` or `$1` inside `value` refers to a capture group. If that group does not exist, it expands to an empty string, so the text you meant to insert silently disappears. To get a literal `$`, write it as `$$`. Alternatively, pass `literal=True` when you do not need a regex pattern.
note.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"t": ["5 dollars", "7 dollars"]})
out = df.select(
    wrong=pl.col("t").str.replace("dollars", "$US"),
    escaped=pl.col("t").str.replace("dollars", "$$US"),
    literal=pl.col("t").str.replace("dollars", "$US", literal=True),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))
